## Proof

**Answer leak check:** The problem statement contains no leaked solution, answer value, proof sketch, or formalization hints. Proceeding.

**Claim.** The set of equivalence classes of well-orders on $\mathbb{N}$ under order-isomorphism has cardinality $\aleph_1$.

---

### Step 1. Equivalence classes biject with order types

For a well-order $R$ on $\mathbb{N}$, the structure $(\mathbb{N},R)$ is a well-ordered set, hence by the basic theory of ordinals it is order-isomorphic to a unique ordinal $\alpha$, called its **order type**:
$$\operatorname{otp}(\mathbb{N},R)=\alpha \iff (\mathbb{N},R)\cong (\alpha,\in).$$
Uniqueness of $\alpha$ is the rigidity/trichotomy theorem for ordinals: two ordinals are order-isomorphic iff they are equal. Consequently
$$R\equiv R' \iff \operatorname{otp}(\mathbb{N},R)=\operatorname{otp}(\mathbb{N},R'),$$
so the map $[R]\mapsto \operatorname{otp}(\mathbb{N},R)$ is a **well-defined injection** from the set of equivalence classes into the class of ordinals.

### Step 2. The image is exactly the set of countable ordinals

Since $(\mathbb{N},R)$ has underlying set $\mathbb{N}$, its order type $\alpha$ satisfies $|\alpha|=|\mathbb{N}|=\aleph_0$ when $\alpha$ is infinite, and $|\alpha|<\aleph_0$ when $\alpha$ is finite. In either case $\alpha$ is **countable**, i.e. $\alpha<\omega_1$, where $\omega_1$ is the least uncountable ordinal. Thus every order type arising is a countable ordinal.

Conversely, let $\alpha<\omega_1$ be any countable ordinal. By definition of "countable ordinal" there exists a bijection $f:\mathbb{N}\to\alpha$. Define a relation $R_\alpha$ on $\mathbb{N}$ by
$$n\;R_\alpha\;m \iff f(n)\in f(m).$$
Pulling back the well-order $(\alpha,\in)$ along the bijection $f$ makes $R_\alpha$ a well-order on $\mathbb{N}$ with $\operatorname{otp}(\mathbb{N},R_\alpha)=\alpha$. Hence **every** countable ordinal is realized as an order type of some well-order on $\mathbb{N}$.

Combining Steps 1 and 2, the equivalence classes of well-orders on $\mathbb{N}$ are in **bijection** with the set
$$\omega_1=\{\alpha\in\mathbf{Ord}:\alpha\text{ is countable}\}.$$

### Step 3. Cardinality of $\omega_1$

By definition $\omega_1$ is the least uncountable ordinal, so its cardinality is
$$|\omega_1|=\aleph_1.$$
(Equivalently: $\omega_1$ is uncountable, and every $\alpha<\omega_1$ is countable, so $|\omega_1|$ is the smallest cardinal strictly larger than every countable cardinal, namely $\aleph_1$.)

### Step 4. Consistency check (no cardinal collapses)

One might worry that the *collection of all well-orders on $\mathbb{N}$* is too large to index $\omega_1$. But the set of all binary relations on $\mathbb{N}$ is $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N})$, which has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$. The well-orders form a subset, so there are at most $2^{\aleph_0}$ of them, and at most $2^{\aleph_0}$ equivalence classes. This is consistent with $\aleph_1\le 2^{\aleph_0}$ (Cantor). The bijection constructed above shows the number of classes is *exactly* $\aleph_1$, independent of the value of the continuum.

---

### Conclusion

The set of equivalence classes of well-orders on $\mathbb{N}$ under order-isomorphism is in bijection with $\omega_1$, the set of all countable ordinals. Therefore its cardinality is

$$\boxed{\aleph_1}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
